notes.text: I will — This is spoken in the person of the church. Garments, &c. - With salvation as with a garment, and with righteousness as with a robe.

Righteousness — His great work of salvation shall break out and appear. Praise - As the natural product, and fruit of it. A prayer of the watchmen for the church in confidence of God's gracious designs and promises to it, ver. 1-12.

Zion's sake — Zion and Jerusalem are both put for the church, Heb. xii, 22. My peace - These seem to be the words of the prophet strongly resolving, notwithstanding all difficulties, to solicit God for the church's happiness, and constantly excite to the belief of it by his preaching, though it were long before it came, for Isaiah lived near two hundred years before this was accomplished. Righteousness - With reference to the Babylonians, understand it of the righteousness of God, who hath promised his people deliverance, and he must be righteous, and so understand salvation before; or rather, the vindicating of his people's cause in the eyes of the nations by the ruin of the Babylonians; he will shew that his people have a righteous cause. Lamp - And to that purpose is set up where it may be seen continually, to signify how eminently conspicuous this prosperous estate of the church should be among the nations, and as it may particularly relate to revealing of Christ unto the world.

A new name — The church shall be more renowned than ever, both in respect of her condition, and so called Hephzi-bah, and of her relation, and so called Beulah, and this new name the Lord gives them accordingly, ver. 4.

Crown of glory — An expression to set forth the dignity of her state. In the hand - Preserved and defended by God's hand. Royal diadem - The same thing with the former for substance. Or, the royal priesthood, whereof the apostle speaks, 1 Pet. ii, 9.

glossa.text:
*Rejoicing I will rejoice* in the Lord, not in the world.

*With the garments of salvation:* with the virtues, with Christ himself, etc., *as far as* yet the Church is one in the head and in the members.

*And as a bride.* He sets forth the examples of another comparison, of which the former is referred to the bridegroom, the latter to the bride.
*And praise:* his own, etc., *as far as* he shall render to the Lord the fruit of praise and of good working.

*For Sion's sake.* ((HIER.)) The prophet in his own person, exceedingly gladdened by all those things which the incarnate Son confers upon the world. And this is it: *For Sion's sake I will not hold my peace,* however much he forbid him to speak, however much he threaten death.

*Let a lamp be kindled.* *Lampas* in Greek, *flamma* in Latin; whence: *I am come to cast fire upon the earth, and what will I but that it burn?* Set alight by this, the apostles spoke with divers tongues.
*A new name.* ((ID.)) It is the custom of the Hebrews to impose new names from new things, etc., *as far as* likewise first Simon, afterwards Peter.
*A crown of glory.* Of the faithful coming from all the parts of the world, as it were a crown.

notes.text: Heavens of heavens — Ye highest heavens, the place of God's throne. Waters - Ye clouds which are above a part of the heavens.
Established — He hath made them constant and incorruptible, not changeable, as the things of the lower world. A decree - Concerning their continuance.
Dragons — Either serpents, which hide in the deep caverns of the earth; or whales, and other sea-monsters, which dwell in the depths of the sea.

Fire — Lightnings and other fireworks of the air. Vapor - Or, fumes: hot exhalations. Fulfilling his word - Executing his commands, either for the comfort or punishment of the inhabitants of the earth.
Above — Above all the glories which are in earth and in heaven.

The horn — In scripture commonly denotes strength, victory, glory, and felicity. An exhortation to praise God for his love to his people, ver. 1-5. And for enabling them to overcome their enemies, ver. 6- 9.

glossa.text: *Praise ye the Lord from the heavens.* ((CASS.)) By the mention of a few he exhorts the whole creation to praise God. There are certain things which have a spirit of praising God in that affection wherewith God pleases them: certain have no understanding, but because they themselves are good in their own order, and are referred to the beauty of the whole, they praise not of themselves, but by them God is praised through those that consider them: and so after a sort they praise, because from them the praise of God is born in us, whereto the prophet here admonishes us.

*For he spoke, and they were made.* ((CASS.)) This against those who say that the world is coeternal with God; there follows: *He commanded.* By his word, and they were created. First he said, *made,* afterward *created.* For make we also can, but not create. He therefore alone creates, which is proper to the Godhead. Praise from his works

*He hath established.* From his power he is almighty, whose works are not changed.

*Unto the age, and unto the age of the age.* ((CAS.)) And though the heaven be new, yet they are said to be well established by God, which are made new through Christ and remain bettered. And here is praise from his power.

*Praise ye the Lady *Dominam*; read *Dominum*, "the Lord".* The second part, where, the heavenly things being enumerated, he descends to earthly things. Turning therefore to them, as exhorting us that by the consideration of them we may praise God, which things considered lay open the praise of God, he says: O ye that are of the earth. *All ye deeps.* *ubyssi* ((AUG.)) The depth of the waters, etc., *as far as* these therefore, that is, he exhorts us to praise by the consideration of them.

*Which do his word.* This therefore because it seemed to certain men that God ruled the higher things, but despised these lower ones, and that they were ruled by chance; but these also God does, and in these least things he is praised, and alleluia is sung.

*Confession.* ((CAS.)) Above he spoke first of heaven, afterward of earth; here of all together. And he takes by heaven all higher things, and by earth all lower things. ((AUG.)) *His confession above heaven and earth.* All things confess him in themselves or in others; the beauty of all things is the voice of them that confess, in those who consider them, that is, let those who consider praise him, both from earthly and from heavenly things, than which there is nothing better.
*He hath exalted the horn of his people.* ((ID.)) Behold what Aggeus and Zacharias prophesied. Now the horn of his people is lowly in tribulations, but when the Lord shall come, it shall be exalted.

notes.text: But when the fulness of the time — Appointed by the Father, ver. 2. Was come, God sent forth - From his own bosom. His Son, miraculously made of the substance of a woman - A virgin, without the concurrence of a man. Made under the law - Both under the precept, and under the curse, of it.
To redeem those under the law — From the curse of it, and from that low, servile state. That we - Jews who believe. Might receive the adoption - All the privileges of adult sons.

And because ye — Gentiles who believe, are also thus made his adult sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts likewise, crying, Abba, Father - Enabling you to call upon God both with the confidence, and the tempers, of dutiful children. The Hebrew and Greek word are joined together, to express the joint cry of the Jews and gentiles.

Wherefore thou — Who believest in Christ. Art no more a servant - Like those who are under the law. But a son - Of mature age. And if a son, then an heir of all the promises, and of the all- sufficient God himself.

glossa.text:
*The fulness of time came.* That is, after that whole space was fulfilled through which the law was to endure, then God sent, etc. *The fulness of time.* He knew when he ought to come, or even to suffer, etc. For there is no hour of his, or of ours, save his will. Yet before it a long series of heralds had to be sent ahead.

*God sent his Son.* Whence, *I went forth from the Father, and came into this world ((Joan. XVI))*. And yet of him John the Evangelist says: *He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not ((Ibid. I))*. Then he joins: *He came unto his own.* Thither therefore was he sent, where he was. Whence also the Prophet says that: *I fill heaven and earth ((Jer. XXIII))* . It is to be asked therefore how that sending is to be understood. If therefore we think soberly of the Son of God the things that are worthy, we ought to understand him to have been sent for this reason, because out of that incomprehensible and unutterable secret of the deep majesty the Word of God gave himself to be comprehended by our minds, not only when he emptied himself, but also when he dwelt among us. *Of a woman.* The usage of the Hebrew tongue calls women not those that are corrupted, but females. *Made under the law.* That he might appear circumcised, as a son of Abraham having the sign of him to whom he had been promised; in whom circumcision was fulfilled: and so let the sign now cease. For Abraham believed that he should have a son, in whom all nations should be blessed: which we believe to be already done.

*That the adoption.* That is, that we might be partakers of the divine glory. For as he himself partakes by nature, so he adopts us unto the seeing of it. For hence we receive adoption, that that only Son of God did not disdain a partaking of our nature, made of a woman, that he might not only be the only-begotten, but might also be made the first-born among many brethren. But he says adoption, that we may distinctly understand the only Son of God.

*God sent.* For that we might be proved to have been adopted by God unto sons, he gave us his Spirit who should show the sign of the Father toward the sons, that, because we should not dare to say this by our infirmity and unworthiness, he might prompt us to dare to say it. *The Spirit of the Son.* Note that the Spirit is the Son's also. And note here also the Trinity. ((AUG.)) If perchance anyone should ask whether the Spirit proceeds from the Son, etc., *as far as* he has from him, that from him also the Holy Spirit should proceed.

*Crying.* It is to be noted that in the Scriptures a cry is understood not as the sending forth of a great voice, but as the greatness of knowledge and of doctrines.

*Abba father.* Elegantly he set down two words signifying the same thing, on account of the whole people which out of Jews and Gentiles has been called into the unity of faith, that the word of the Hebrews might pertain to the Hebrews, the Greek to the Gentiles. But the same signification of each word pertains to the unity of the same faith and Spirit.

*Who by nature are not,* etc. He shows that the nature of the true God is one, namely of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. But what is it to be God by nature, save to be true God? Whence elsewhere the Apostle: *You are converted to serve the living and true God ((I Petr. II))* .

notes.text: The days — The forty days prescribed, Lev. xii, 2, 4.
Exod. xiii, 2.
A pair of turtle doves, or two young pigeons — This offering sufficed for the poor. Lev. xii, 8.
The consolation of Israel — A common phrase for the Messiah, who was to be the everlasting consolation of the Israel of God. The Holy Ghost was upon him - That is, he was a prophet.
By the Spirit — By a particular Revelation or impulse from him.
Thy salvation — Thy Christ, thy saviour.
And the glory of thy people Israel — For after the Gentiles are enlightened, all Israel shall be saved.
Joseph and his mother marvelled at those things which were spoken — For they did not thoroughly understand them.

Simeon blessed them — Joseph and Mary. This child is set for the fall and rising again of many - That is, he will be a savour of death to some, to unbelievers: a savour of life to others, to believers: and for a sign which shall be spoken against - A sign from God, yet rejected of men: but the time for declaring this at large was not yet come: that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed - The event will be, that by means of that contradiction, the inmost thoughts of many, whether good or bad, will be made manifest.
A sword shall pierce through thy own soul — So it did, when he suffered: particularly at his crucifixion.

Fourscore and four years — These were the years of her life, not her widowhood only. Who departed not from the temple - Who attended there at all the stated hours of prayer. But served God with fastings and prayers - Even at that age. Night and day - That is, spending therein a considerable part of the night, as well as of the day.

To all that were waiting for redemption — The scepter now appeared to be departing from Judah, though it was not actually gone: Daniel's weeks were plainly near their period. And the revival of the spirit of prophecy, together with the memorable occurrences relating to the birth of John the Baptist, and of Jesus, could not but encourage and quicken the expectation of pious persons at this time. Let the example of these aged saints animate those, whose hoary heads, like theirs, are a crown of glory, being found in the way of righteousness. Let those venerable lips, so soon to be silent in the grave, be now employed in the praises of their Redeemer. Let them labour to leave those behind, to whom Christ will be as precious as he has been to them; and who will be waiting for God's salvation, when they are gone to enjoy it.

And the child grew — In bodily strength and stature; and waxed strong in spirit - The powers of his human mind daily improved; filled with wisdom - By the light of the indwelling Spirit, which gradually opened itself in his soul; and the grace of God was upon him - That is, the peculiar favour of God rested upon him, even as man.

glossa.text: *They carried him.* The little ones who from the whole kingdom of the Jews were carried to the temple, if they were of the tribe of Levi, were kept back perpetually for the ministry of the house. If of another tribe, the firstborn were redeemed by a price given by their parents, to be carried back to their own homes.
*As it is written. ((BEDA.))* It is written in the law: *A woman who, having received,* etc., *as far as* she enters upon the joys of heavenly blessedness with the fruits of good works.
*A pair of turtledoves. ((ID.))* This was the offering of the poor, who were not able to offer a lamb, so that in all things the humility of the Lord might be plain.

*And behold there was a man.* Not only the angels, but every age and sex render testimony to the child that is born. And as he was foretold by the faithful of all ages, so at his coming he is proclaimed with the praise of all the saints.

*The child.* Since boyhood begins after the seven years of infancy, Jesus is frequently called a child, not so much for his age as for his service; whence the Prophet: *Behold my child,* because *the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister ((Isa. XLII)).*

*Now thou dost dismiss thy servant. ((AMBR.))* He who wishes to be dismissed, let him come into Jerusalem, etc., *as far as* then he shall be dismissed so that he may not see death, because he had seen life.

*Behold this child is set.* For the ruin of those who had stood, and the resurrection of those who had fallen; or for the ruin of vices, and for the resurrection of virtues. Not in himself alone, but in his preachers also is he set for ruin and resurrection; whence the Apostle: *We are the good odour of Christ unto God, in them that are saved, and in them that perish.* For by the good odour some are saved, others perish ((II Cor. II)).

*A sword. ((BEDA.))* The sorrow of the Lord's passion, etc., *as far as* she beholds the cockle springing up.

*That may be revealed.* Before, it was uncertain which of the Jews would receive the grace of Christ, and which would spit upon it: but at the hearing of the nativity the thoughts are revealed, and Herod and others are troubled, while certain men come to the teaching of Christ.

*And there was Anna,* etc. Because through a man and a woman the life of the whole world was lost, in the testimony of life returning through Christ Anna is joined to Simeon. It agrees with the mysteries of the Church that Anna is interpreted grace, who is the daughter of Phanuel, who is called the face of God; whence above: *The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us ((Psal. IV))*. *Of the tribe of Aser.* That is, of the blessed, she is descended, from him who among the twelve patriarchs is eighth in the order of birth, on account of the mystery of the resurrection. There are five Annas. The first the mother of Samuel, the second the wife of Raguel, the third the mother of Tobias, the fourth the daughter of Phanuel, the fifth the mother of Mary.

*She had advanced in days. ((BEDA.))* According to the history, Anna, and of a devout manner of life, etc., *as far as* they are multiplied on account of the apostolic teaching.

*To all who,* etc. To all the faithful who, weighed down by the yoke of the foreigner Herod, were awaiting the deliverance of the city and of the people, she promised through the coming of Christ a redemption close at hand from the tyranny of the stranger.
*And the child. ((BEDA.))* In that he was a child, etc., *as far as* he had begun to be made man, he was perfect as God.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,
echoes.note: The cluster of sonship/adoption/firstborn language (vv.5-7, 'receive the adoption,' 'no longer a bondservant but a son,' 'heir') recalls God's claim 'Israel is my son, my firstborn.' Coherence is high in a redemption-from-bondage argument that runs on Exodus categories; Recurrence of son/heir terms supports it. Verbal volume is moderate, hence allusion not quotation.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: "God sent out his Son, born to a woman" (v.4) faintly evokes the protoevangelium's promise of the woman's seed who undoes the serpent. Coherence with Paul's redemption-of-the-enslaved theme is real but the verbal volume is thin; the phrase 'born of woman' is a common idiom (cf. Job). Marked low and contested.

echoes.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'Out of Egypt I called my son' supplies the same divine sonship motif undergirding 'God sent out his Son' and the adoption of children. The link is conceptual rather than verbal in Galatians; availability and coherence hold but volume is low. Contested as a deliberate echo.

echoes.text: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:
echoes.note: 'That he might redeem those who were under the law' (v.5) draws on the Exodus vocabulary of God redeeming a people from slavery (cf. Exod 6:6, 15:13). The redemption-from-bondage frame coheres tightly with Paul's slave/son contrast, but no single Exodus verse is quoted, so this is a diffuse echo.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “‘When the days of her purification are completed, for a son, or for a daughter, she shall bring to the priest at the door of the Tent of Meeting, a year old lamb for a burnt offering, and a young pigeon, or a turtledove, for a sin offering:
echoes.note: 'The days of their purification according to the law of Moses' are exactly Leviticus 12's prescription for the mother's purification after childbirth, culminating in a burnt offering and a sin offering. Volume and availability are maximal since Luke is paraphrasing the statute; coherence is total.

echoes.text: If she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves, or two young pigeons; the one for a burnt offering, and the other for a sin offering: and the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean.’”
echoes.note: Luke quotes the offering 'a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons,' the Levitical concession for those who cannot afford a lamb. This is the explicit nearer source of v. 24's citation and signals the holy family's poverty; it is a near-verbatim quotation introduced by 'as is said in the law.'

echoes.text: “Sanctify to me all of the firstborn, whatever opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and of animal. It is mine.”
echoes.note: 'Every male who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord' renders the consecration of the firstborn, 'sanctify to me every firstborn that opens the womb.' Luke marks it 'as it is written,' so this is a formal quotation; the firstborn-belongs-to-God theme tracks the prototokos of v. 7.

echoes.text: that you shall set apart to Yahweh all that opens the womb, and every firstborn which you have that comes from an animal. The males shall be Yahweh’s. Every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb; and if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck; and you shall redeem all the firstborn of man among your sons. It shall be, when your son asks you in time to come, saying, ‘What is this?’ that you shall tell him, ‘By strength of hand […]
echoes.note: The presentation of the firstborn to the Lord enacts the Exodus mandate to set apart every firstborn that opens the womb because the LORD spared Israel's firstborn at the Passover. Coherence is exact and the redemptive backstory (firstborn spared by blood) resonates with Luke's larger soteriology.

echoes.text: Everything that opens the womb, of all flesh which they offer to Yahweh, both of man and animal shall be yours. Nevertheless, you shall surely redeem the firstborn of man, and you shall redeem the firstborn of unclean animals. You shall redeem those who are to be redeemed of them from a month old, according to your estimation, for five shekels of money, after the shekel of the sanctuary, which weighs twenty gerahs.
echoes.note: The redemption of the firstborn human (to be redeemed at a set price) underlies bringing Jesus 'to present him to the Lord'; Numbers spells out that every firstborn is the LORD's and must be redeemed. This is the priestly legislation completing the Exodus firstborn command Luke invokes.

echoes.text: When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, with three bulls, and one ephah of meal, and a bottle of wine, and brought him to Yahweh’s house in Shiloh. The child was young. They killed the bull, and brought the child to Eli. She said, “Oh, my lord, as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to Yahweh. For this child I prayed; and Yahweh has given me my petition which I asked of him. Therefore also I have granted him […]
echoes.note: Bringing the child up to the sanctuary and presenting him 'to the Lord' strongly recalls Hannah bringing Samuel and 'lending' him to the LORD; Luke's whole infancy narrative is patterned on 1 Samuel (Magnificat on Hannah's song). Recurrence of the Samuel template gives this real weight beyond the bare legal citations.

echoes.text: “All that opens the womb is mine; and all your livestock that is male, the firstborn of cow and sheep. The firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb: and if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck. All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. No one shall appear before me empty.
echoes.note: The restated covenant law that 'all that opens the womb is mine' and the firstborn must be redeemed reinforces v. 23's quotation; the doublet across Exodus 13 and 34 supplies recurrence for the firstborn-consecration theme Luke foregrounds.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: When 'they brought him up to Jerusalem... to the temple,' Luke begins to stage Malachi's promise that 'the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple,' a theme that climaxes in Simeon and Anna meeting him there. The temple-arrival coherence is strong and recurs through vv. 25-38, though it is set up rather than quoted here.

echoes.text: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.
echoes.note: Simeon is 'looking for the consolation (paraklesis) of Israel,' the exact Septuagintal keynote of Isaiah's 'Comfort, comfort my people.' Volume is high (the noun consolation), the Isaiah background recurs throughout the Nunc Dimittis, and coherence is exact: the end of exile-comfort arrives in the child.

echoes.text: Yahweh has made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
echoes.note: 'My eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples' renders Isaiah's 'all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God,' where the LORD bares his arm 'before all the nations.' The seeing-of-God's-salvation-before-all-nations cluster is verbally and thematically exact.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: 'A light for revelation to the nations (Gentiles), and the glory of your people Israel' fuses the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' with Israel's restoration. Volume and coherence are very high; this is among the clearest OT echoes in the chapter.

echoes.text: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations;
echoes.note: The Servant given 'as a light to the nations' (and a covenant to the people) directly informs Simeon's 'light for revelation to the nations.' The doublet with Isaiah 49:6 supplies recurrence; the universal-light-of-salvation theme coheres exactly with Luke's program of salvation reaching the Gentiles.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”
echoes.note: Simeon's oracle that the child is 'set for the falling and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign spoken against' draws on Isaiah's stone that becomes 'a sanctuary, but a stone of offense... many shall stumble and fall.' The fall/rise division of Israel over the sign is verbally and thematically coherent, a key prophetic warrant for Luke's divided-Israel theme.

echoes.text: but you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried in a good old age.
echoes.note: 'Now you are releasing your servant... in peace; for my eyes have seen...' draws on the promise that Abraham would 'go to his fathers in peace' once God's word was fulfilled. The depart-in-peace-after-seeing-the-promise pattern is coherent, supplying the form of Simeon's release.

echoes.text: Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive.”
echoes.note: Simeon's readiness to die having seen salvation closely parallels Jacob: 'Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive.' The see-then-ready-to-die formula is verbally and thematically close, a strong candidate alongside Genesis 15:15 for the source of the Nunc Dimittis opening.

echoes.text: I bring near my righteousness, it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not wait; and I will place salvation in Zion for Israel my glory.
echoes.note: 'I will put salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory' supplies the second half of Simeon's couplet, 'the glory of your people Israel,' pairing salvation with Israel's glory. The salvation-and-glory-of-Israel coherence and Septuagintal availability make this a solid supporting allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together; for the mouth of Yahweh has spoken it.”
echoes.note: Simeon's 'my eyes have seen your salvation... before the face of all peoples' echoes 'the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together.' The universal-seeing-of-revealed-glory theme reinforces the broader Isaiah 40-55 matrix of the Nunc Dimittis.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: The 'sign spoken against' over which many fall and rise also draws on the tested cornerstone laid in Zion, which becomes the criterion of standing or stumbling. Paired with Isaiah 8 this supplies the stone-of-decision motif; coherence is strong though Luke does not quote it.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: Simeon meets the child precisely in the temple, fulfilling 'the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple,' which Malachi pairs with a refining that tests Israel, coherent with the falling-and-rising oracle. The temple-coming-as-test theme recurs with Anna in the next pericope, giving it recurrence.

echoes.text: It shall be said in that day, “Behold, this is our God! We have waited for him, and he will save us! This is Yahweh! We have waited for him. We will be glad and rejoice in his salvation!”
echoes.note: 'This is our God; we have waited for him... let us be glad in his salvation' parallels the waiting Simeon who finally sees God's salvation. The wait-then-rejoice-in-salvation pattern is coherent, though it is a faint supporting echo within the strong Isaianic cluster.

echoes.text: Or if I bring a sword on that land, and say, Sword, go through the land; so that I cut off from it man and animal;
echoes.note: The 'sword' that 'will pierce through your own soul' has been linked to Ezekiel's recurring 'a sword shall pass through the land,' a figure of sifting judgment that divides. The sword-of-division imagery coheres with the falling-and-rising oracle, though the application to Mary's soul is distinctively Lukan, so the source is faint.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
echoes.note: The piercing 'sword' anticipating grief over the child has been read against Zechariah's 'they shall look on me whom they have pierced, and mourn,' associated with a future piercing of the LORD's chosen. The piercing-and-mourning link is suggestive but indirect here, hence a contested faint echo.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

echoes.text: Their sword shall enter into their own heart. Their bows shall be broken.
echoes.note: 'A sword will pierce through your own soul' may color itself with the psalm's idiom that the wicked's 'sword shall enter their own heart.' The sword-into-the-soul phrasing offers verbal contact, but the sense differs (Mary's anguish vs. the wicked's self-destruction), so the echo is faint.

echoes.text: Judith was a widow in her house three years and four months. She made herself a tent upon the roof of her house, and put on sackcloth upon her loins. The garments of her widowhood were upon her. And she fasted all the days of her widowhood, except the eves of the Sabbaths, the Sabbaths, the eves of the new moons, the new moons, and the feasts and joyful days of the house of Israel. She was of a goodly countenance, and exceeding beautiful to behold. Her […]
echoes.note: Anna, a long-widowed woman of great age devoted to fasting and prayer, closely matches Judith, a widow who lived chastely many years, fasted often, and feared God greatly. The pious-aged-widow type is coherent and the fasting-and-prayer detail gives real volume; Luke seems to draw on the Second-Temple ideal Judith exemplifies.

echoes.text: Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand; and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dances.
echoes.note: Anna is introduced as 'a prophetess' (prophetis), the same title and role given to Miriam who leads Israel's praise. The prophetess-who-leads-thanksgiving pattern is coherent, situating Anna in the line of Israel's women prophets.

echoes.text: Break out into joy, sing together, you waste places of Jerusalem; for Yahweh has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem.
echoes.note: Anna speaks of the child 'to all who were looking for the redemption (lytrosis) of Jerusalem,' echoing Isaiah's 'the LORD has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem.' The redemption-of-Jerusalem phrase has direct Septuagintal availability and pairs with Simeon's 'consolation of Israel,' giving the pericope a strong Isaianic frame.

echoes.text: Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, she judged Israel at that time.
echoes.note: Anna 'the prophetess' also recalls Deborah, 'a prophetess... judging Israel,' another woman bearing the prophetic office at a hinge of salvation history. The title link is real but generic across the female-prophet category, so it is a faint supporting echo to Miriam.

echoes.text: “Speak comfortably to Jerusalem; and call out to her that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received of Yahweh’s hand double for all her sins.”
echoes.note: 'Looking for the redemption of Jerusalem' also resonates with Isaiah's address to Jerusalem that her warfare is ended and iniquity pardoned. It belongs to the same Isaiah 40-52 consolation matrix as Simeon's oracle; faint as an independent source but coherent with the cluster.

echoes.text: She vowed a vow, and said, “Yahweh of Armies, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your handmaid, and remember me, and not forget your handmaid, but will give to your handmaid a boy, then I will give him to Yahweh all the days of his life, and no razor shall come on his head.”
echoes.note: Anna's name is the Greek form of Hannah, and her temple devotion of fasting and prayer mirrors Hannah's vow and worship at the sanctuary; Luke's infancy narrative is steeped in the Hannah/Samuel story. The onomastic and devotional link is suggestive though not pressed, so a faint echo.

echoes.text: The child Samuel grew on, and increased in favor both with Yahweh, and also with men.
echoes.note: 'The child was growing, and was becoming strong... filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him' closely follows the boy Samuel who 'continued to grow... in favor with the LORD and with men.' The growth-and-favor formula is verbally and structurally parallel, and recurs at v. 52, giving strong recurrence within the chapter.

echoes.text: The woman bore a son, and named him Samson: and the child grew, and Yahweh blessed him.
echoes.note: 'The child grew, and the LORD blessed him' (Samson) supplies the same OT growth-of-the-promised-child notice that Luke reuses; together with 1 Samuel 2:26 it shows the type-scene of the divinely favored child maturing. Coherence with the annunciation-and-birth pattern is high.

echoes.text: but he said to me, ‘Behold, you shall conceive, and bear a son; and now drink no wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing; for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.’”
echoes.note: That the child is 'filled with wisdom' and grows under God's grace faintly recalls the Nazirite child set apart to God from the womb in the Samson cycle; the link is the consecrated-child motif, supportive of the Samson allusion but not independently strong.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Praise the Lord from the heavens.
Sun and moon, shining stars, praise his name.
Old Simeon took the child in his arms.
My eyes have seen your salvation.
A light for revelation to the nations.
And glory for your people.
Come, let us worship with all creation.
Glory to God in the highest! Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: He had waited a long lifetime in that temple, and when they brought the child in, old Simeon reached out and took him in his arms.
Glory to God in the highest!
Now you let your servant go in peace, he said, for my own eyes have seen the salvation you prepared.
Glory to God in the highest!
A light to the nations, a glory for your people — and Anna, eighty-four and faithful, told everyone who would listen.
Glory to God in the highest!
So we come with the old and the waiting and the young, and we lift our praise with sun and moon and stars.
Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth! Amen.

lines: Praise him, sun and moon and shining stars.

My eyes have seen your salvation, he says.
Glory to God in the highest!
Come, let us worship the light of the nations.
Glory to God in the highest! Amen.
